## 11. Heterogeneous Silicon Placement, AXI Bus QoS Arbiters, and Thermodynamic Junction Heating

In Physical AI systems, cognitive stages are partitioned across heterogeneous silicon fabrics based on execution cadence, memory access patterns, and thermal dissipation envelopes. This section establishes the mathematical formulations governing shared interconnect bus arbitration, arithmetic intensity rooflines, and dynamic junction temperature evolution.

### AXI Bus Quality-of-Service Priority Arbitration

In Unified Memory Architecture (UMA) Systems-on-Chip, heterogeneous masters (CPU cores, Neural Processing Units, and direct-memory-access camera peripherals) issue concurrent read and write bursts across a shared AXI interconnect crossbar.

Let $\mathcal{M} = \{1, \dots, M\}$ denote the set of bus masters contending for memory crossbar bandwidth $B_{\text{total}}$ ($\text{GB/s}$). Each transaction from master $m \in \mathcal{M}$ carries a 4-bit Quality-of-Service priority value $q_m \in \{0, 1, \dots, 15\}$, where $q = 15$ designates the highest real-time priority.

The effective service latency $L_m$ for a memory read request of size $S_m$ bytes from master $m$ under weighted priority arbitration is modeled by:

$$L_m = \tau_{\text{arb}} + \frac{S_m}{B_{\text{crossbar}}} + \sum_{k \in \mathcal{M}, q_k > q_m} \frac{S_k}{B_{\text{crossbar}}} + \mathbb{I}(q_m < 15) \cdot \tau_{\text{burst\_in\_flight}}$$

where:
* $\tau_{\text{arb}}$: Crossbar arbitration switching latency (typically $4\text{--}12\text{ ns}$).
* $\tau_{\text{burst\_in\_flight}}$: Latency penalty incurred when waiting for an ongoing atomic non-preemptible burst from a lower-priority master to conclude ($S_{\text{burst}} / B_{\text{crossbar}}$).

To guarantee that real-time microcontroller reads ($1000\text{ Hz}$ safety loops) never miss control deadlines, the silicon arbiter enforces hard preemption for $q_{\text{MCU}} = 15$:

$$L_{\text{MCU}} \le \tau_{\text{arb}} + \frac{S_{\text{payload}}}{B_{\text{crossbar}}} + \frac{S_{\text{burst\_max}}}{B_{\text{crossbar}}} \le 50.0\text{ ns}$$

For background camera sensor DMA streams ($q_{\text{cam}} = 4$), transactions are admitted only during bus idle cycles when higher-priority queues ($q \ge 10$) are empty.

### Arithmetic Intensity and the Memory Power Roofline

The computational efficiency of an embedded neural model is governed by its arithmetic intensity $I_{\text{arith}}$, defined as the ratio of floating-point arithmetic operations to off-chip DRAM memory transfers:

$$I_{\text{arith}} = \frac{N_{\text{FLOPs}}}{N_{\text{Bytes\_DRAM}}} \quad \left[ \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Byte}} \right]$$

Total electrical power dissipated by the compute subsystem $P_{\text{compute}}$ is the sum of dynamic gate switching power, static transistor leakage, and DRAM bus input/output pad driving power:

$$P_{\text{compute}} = P_{\text{dynamic}} + P_{\text{leakage}} + P_{\text{DRAM\_IO}}$$

$$P_{\text{dynamic}} = \alpha \cdot C_{\text{eff}} \cdot V_{\text{core}}^2 \cdot f_{\text{clock}}$$

$$P_{\text{DRAM\_IO}} = E_{\text{DRAM\_byte}} \cdot \text{BW}_{\text{DRAM}} = E_{\text{DRAM\_byte}} \cdot \frac{\text{Throughput}_{\text{FLOPs/s}}}{I_{\text{arith}}}$$

where $E_{\text{DRAM\_byte}} \approx 150\text{ pJ/Byte}$ for off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM, compared to $E_{\text{SRAM\_byte}} \approx 2\text{ pJ/Byte}$ for on-chip static SRAM.

* **SRAM Model Tiling Invariant:** When trajectory decoders are quantized to INT8 and fit entirely within on-chip SRAM ($N_{\text{Bytes\_DRAM}} \to 0$), $I_{\text{arith}} \to \infty$. DRAM power collapses ($P_{\text{DRAM\_IO}} \to 0$), reducing total inference energy consumption by up to $98.5\%$.

### Continuous 3D Heat Diffusion PDE and Multi-Layer Thermal RC Discretization

In dense embedded packaging, heat generated by active transistor switching and memory bus driving diffuses through a multi-layer physical stack (Silicon Die $\to$ Thermal Interface Material $\to$ Copper Heat Spreader $\to$ Aluminum Enclosure). The continuous thermal evolution across space $\mathbf{r} = (x, y, z) \in \Omega$ and time $t \ge 0$ is governed by the 3D anisotropic heat diffusion partial differential equation:

$$\rho(\mathbf{r}) c_p(\mathbf{r}) \frac{\partial T(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t} = \nabla \cdot \left( k(\mathbf{r}) \nabla T(\mathbf{r}, t) \right) + \dot{q}_v(\mathbf{r}, t)$$

where:
* $\rho(\mathbf{r})$: Material density ($\text{kg/m}^3$).
* $c_p(\mathbf{r})$: Specific heat capacity ($\text{J}/(\text{kg}\cdot\text{K})$).
* $k(\mathbf{r})$: Thermal conductivity tensor ($\text{W}/(\text{m}\cdot\text{K})$).
* $\dot{q}_v(\mathbf{r}, t)$: Volumetric heat generation rate ($\text{W/m}^3$), localized to the active silicon junction layer ($0 \le z \le d_{\text{active}}$) such that $\int_{V_{\text{die}}} \dot{q}_v dV = P_{\text{compute}}(t)$.

Across each physical material interface $z = z_{\text{int}}$, temperature and conductive heat flux satisfy strict boundary continuity:

$$T_i(x, y, z_{\text{int}}, t) = T_{i+1}(x, y, z_{\text{int}}, t), \qquad -k_i \left.\frac{\partial T_i}{\partial z}\right|_{z_{\text{int}}} = -k_{i+1} \left.\frac{\partial T_{i+1}}{\partial z}\right|_{z_{\text{int}}}$$

At the outer chassis boundary $\partial \Omega$, heat dissipates into ambient air via natural convection and radiation (Robin boundary condition):

$$-k_{\text{case}} \left( \nabla T \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \right) = h_{\text{conv}} \left( T(\mathbf{r}, t) - T_{\text{ambient}} \right) + \epsilon \sigma_{\text{SB}} \left( T(\mathbf{r}, t)^4 - T_{\text{ambient}}^4 \right)$$

where $h_{\text{conv}}$ is the convective heat transfer coefficient ($\text{W}/(\text{m}^2\cdot\text{K})$), $\epsilon$ is surface emissivity, and $\sigma_{\text{SB}} = 5.670 \times 10^{-8}\text{ W}/(\text{m}^2\cdot\text{K}^4)$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant.

#### Modal Decomposition to Foster and Cauer RC Ladder Networks

Applying spatial separation of variables $T(\mathbf{r}, t) = T_{\text{ambient}} + \sum_{m=1}^\infty \psi_m(\mathbf{r}) \theta_m(t)$ against orthogonal spatial eigenfunctions $\psi_m(\mathbf{r})$ reduces the infinite-dimensional PDE to a decoupled set of modal thermal time constants $\tau_m = R_m C_m$:

$$\frac{d\theta_m(t)}{dt} = -\frac{1}{\tau_m}\theta_m(t) + \Gamma_m P_{\text{compute}}(t)$$

In the frequency domain, the driving-point thermal impedance $Z_{\text{th}}(s) = \frac{\Delta T_j(s)}{P(s)}$ expands into the **Foster RC Ladder Representation**:

$$Z_{\text{th}}(s) = \sum_{m=1}^N \frac{R_m}{1 + s R_m C_m}$$

Transforming the Foster network via continued-fraction polynomial synthesis yields the physically meaningful **Cauer RC Ladder Topology**, representing direct cascaded physical layers ($(\text{Junction}) \to (\text{Case}) \to (\text{Ambient})$).

### Lumped-Parameter Thermodynamic Junction Differential Equations

Truncating the Cauer ladder to the dominant two-pole network ($N=2$) yields the coupled lumped-parameter system for the silicon junction and chassis:

$$\begin{aligned}
C_{\text{die}} \frac{d T_j(t)}{dt} &= P_{\text{compute}}(t) - \frac{T_j(t) - T_{\text{case}}(t)}{R_{\theta,\text{jc}}} \\
C_{\text{case}} \frac{d T_{\text{case}}(t)}{dt} &= \frac{T_j(t) - T_{\text{case}}(t)}{R_{\theta,\text{jc}}} - \frac{T_{\text{case}}(t) - T_{\text{ambient}}}{R_{\theta,\text{ca}}}
\end{aligned}$$

where:
* $T_j$: Silicon junction temperature ($^\circ\text{C}$).
* $T_{\text{case}}$: Chassis metal case temperature ($^\circ\text{C}$).
* $C_{\text{die}}, C_{\text{case}}$: Thermal heat capacities of the silicon package and aluminum chassis ($\text{J/K}$).
* $R_{\theta,\text{jc}}$: Thermal resistance from junction to case ($\text{K/W}$).
* $R_{\theta,\text{ca}}$: Thermal resistance from case to ambient air ($\text{K/W}$).

Solving the transient step response under constant high-load neural inference power $P_{\text{step}}$:

$$T_j(t) = T_{\text{ambient}} + P_{\text{step}} (R_{\theta,\text{jc}} + R_{\theta,\text{ca}}) \left[ 1 - \frac{\tau_1 e^{-t/\tau_1} - \tau_2 e^{-t/\tau_2}}{\tau_1 - \tau_2} \right]$$

where $\tau_1, \tau_2$ are the dominant thermal time constants of the silicon package ($1\text{--}5\text{ s}$) and the physical chassis ($60\text{--}300\text{ s}$).

* **Proactive Thermal Derating Boundary:** If $T_j(t) \ge T_{\text{warn}} = 75.0^\circ\text{C}$, the firmware triggers proactive cadence scaling ($50\text{ Hz} \to 20\text{ Hz}$, $H=16 \to 32$), dropping $P_{\text{compute}}$ by $55\%$ before junction temperature reaches the destructive hardware DVFS throttling knee ($T_{\text{trip}} = 85.0^\circ\text{C}$).

## 12. Authority State Transition Dynamics and Bumpless Transfer Polynomials

In collaborative and supervisory robotics, physical control authority transfers dynamically between autonomous neural policies and human safety operators. This section formalizes the authority state space, derives $\mathcal{C}^2$ quintic smoothstep blending polynomials, and establishes statistical bounds on policy drift under human intervention.

### The 4-State Authority Machine and Preemption Invariant

Let $\mathcal{S}_{\text{auth}} = \{\text{MANUAL}, \text{SHARED}, \text{AUTONOMOUS}, \text{ESTOP}\}$ denote the set of discrete authority states. State transitions are governed by input event vector $\mathbf{e} = [e_{\text{estop}}, e_{\text{human}}, e_{\text{lease}}, e_{\text{cbf}}]^T \in \{0, 1\}^4$:

$$\delta: \mathcal{S}_{\text{auth}} \times \{0, 1\}^4 \longrightarrow \mathcal{S}_{\text{auth}}$$

The state transition logic is defined by the strict priority hierarchy:

$$\delta(s, \mathbf{e}) = \begin{cases}
\text{ESTOP} & \text{if } e_{\text{estop}} = 1 \\
\text{MANUAL} & \text{if } e_{\text{estop}} = 0 \land e_{\text{human}} = 1 \\
\text{SHARED} & \text{if } e_{\text{estop}} = 0 \land e_{\text{human}} = 0 \land e_{\text{shared\_req}} = 1 \\
\text{AUTONOMOUS} & \text{if } e_{\text{estop}} = 0 \land e_{\text{human}} = 0 \land e_{\text{lease}} = 1 \land e_{\text{cbf}} = 1 \\
\text{ESTOP} & \text{if } s = \text{AUTONOMOUS} \land (e_{\text{lease}} = 0 \lor e_{\text{cbf}} = 0)
\end{cases}$$

Hardware Safe Torque Off lines enforce the preemption invariant: if $e_{\text{estop}} = 1$, gate driver power is physically unlatched within $< 5.0\,\mu\text{s}$, regardless of processor state.

### Derivation of the $\mathcal{C}^2$ Quintic Smoothstep Polynomial

When transitioning between autonomous policy command $\mathbf{u}_{\text{policy}}(t)$ and human operator input $\mathbf{u}_{\text{human}}(t)$ over transition window $T_{\text{blend}} \in [100, 200]\text{ ms}$, the blended command is:

$$\mathbf{u}_{\text{cmd}}(t) = (1 - S(\alpha(t))) \cdot \mathbf{u}_{\text{policy}}(t) + S(\alpha(t)) \cdot \mathbf{u}_{\text{human}}(t)$$

$$\alpha(t) = \frac{t - t_{\text{takeover}}}{T_{\text{blend}}}, \quad \alpha \in [0, 1]$$

To eliminate torque derivative shocks ($\dot{\mathbf{u}} \to \infty$) and mechanical jerk impulses ($\dddot{\mathbf{q}} \to \infty$), the blending polynomial $S(\alpha) = \sum_{k=0}^5 c_k \alpha^k$ must satisfy six physical boundary conditions:

$$\begin{aligned}
S(0) &= 0, \quad &S(1) &= 1 \quad &&(\text{Zero and Unity Amplitudes}) \\
\dot{S}(0) &= 0, \quad &\dot{S}(1) &= 0 \quad &&(\text{Zero Initial and Final Velocities}) \\
\ddot{S}(0) &= 0, \quad &\ddot{S}(1) &= 0 \quad &&(\text{Zero Initial and Final Accelerations})
\end{aligned}$$

Setting $S(0) = \dot{S}(0) = \ddot{S}(0) = 0$ directly forces $c_0 = c_1 = c_2 = 0$. The polynomial simplifies to:

$$S(\alpha) = c_3 \alpha^3 + c_4 \alpha^4 + c_5 \alpha^5$$

Applying the remaining three boundary conditions at $\alpha = 1$:

$$\begin{aligned}
S(1) &= c_3 + c_4 + c_5 = 1 \\
\dot{S}(1) &= 3 c_3 + 4 c_4 + 5 c_5 = 0 \\
\ddot{S}(1) &= 6 c_3 + 12 c_4 + 20 c_5 = 0
\end{aligned}$$

Solving this $3 \times 3$ linear system:

$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & 5 \\ 6 & 12 & 20 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} c_3 \\ c_4 \\ c_5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \implies \begin{bmatrix} c_3 \\ c_4 \\ c_5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ -15 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}$$

The unique $\mathcal{C}^2$ quintic smoothstep polynomial is:

$$S(\alpha) = 6\alpha^5 - 15\alpha^4 + 10\alpha^3$$

The peak derivative occurs at the midpoint $\alpha = 0.5$:

$$\dot{S}_{\text{max}} = \left. (30\alpha^4 - 60\alpha^3 + 30\alpha^2) \right|_{\alpha=0.5} = 30(0.0625) - 60(0.125) + 30(0.25) = 1.875$$

The maximum commanded torque rate of change during human takeover is strictly bounded:

$$\|\dot{\mathbf{u}}_{\text{cmd}}\| \le \frac{1.875}{T_{\text{blend}}} \|\mathbf{u}_{\text{human}} - \mathbf{u}_{\text{policy}}\| + \|\dot{\mathbf{u}}_{\text{policy}}\|$$

For $T_{\text{blend}} = 150.0\text{ ms}$ and a maximum torque discrepancy of $40.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, the peak torque rate is bounded to $\le 500.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/s}$, well within the continuous capability of brushless motor gearboxes.

### Compounding Covariate Shift Bounds Under Behavioral Cloning

When training a policy $\pi_\theta$ via supervised behavioral cloning on logged human teleoperation data $\mathcal{D} = \{(s_t, a_t^*)\}$, let $\epsilon$ denote the expected single-step error rate under the training distribution:

$$\mathbb{E}_{s \sim d_{\pi^*}} \left[ \ell(\pi_\theta(s), \pi^*(s)) \right] \le \epsilon$$

Under autonomous closed-loop execution, small errors shift the state distribution away from the demonstration support. Following Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell [-@ross2011reduction], the compounding total variation distance between the expert state distribution $d_{\pi^*}$ and the learned policy distribution $d_{\pi_\theta}$ over horizon $T$ is bounded by:

$$D_{\text{TV}}(d_{\pi^*}, d_{\pi_\theta}) \le 2 (1 - (1 - \epsilon)^T) \le 2 \epsilon T$$

The cumulative task loss over horizon $T$ compounds quadratically:

$$J(\pi_\theta) \le J(\pi^*) + \epsilon \cdot T^2$$

* **DAgger Policy Gradient Formulation:** To prevent quadratic error compounding, dataset aggregation (DAgger) samples states from the running policy's own induced distribution $d_{\pi_\theta}$ and queries an expert oracle for corrections $a_t^* = \pi^*(s_t)$. Truncating the pre-takeover drift phase prevents the policy from learning spurious associations between dangerous drift and recovery maneuvers.

### Hierarchical Merkle Tree Cryptographic Audit Proofs for Telemetry Flight Recorders

To ensure non-repudiation and microsecond forensic auditability without storing gigabytes of redundant hashes, flight-recorder telemetry frames are structured into a binary Merkle tree.

Let $\mathcal{D} = \{\mathcal{T}_1, \mathcal{T}_2, \dots, \mathcal{T}_N\}$ denote a sequential stream of $N = 2^K$ telemetry frames recorded by the black-box flight recorder.

1. **Leaf Hashes (Level $d=0$):**
   $$h_{0, i} = \text{SHA-256}(\mathcal{T}_i), \quad i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$$

2. **Internal Node Hashes (Levels $d = 1, \dots, K$):**
   $$h_{d, j} = \text{SHA-256}\left( h_{d-1, 2j-1} \,\|\, h_{d-1, 2j} \right), \quad j \in \{1, \dots, 2^{K-d}\}$$

3. **Merkle Root Digest:**
   $$R_N = h_{K, 1} \in \{0, 1\}^{256}$$

#### Logarithmic Membership Verification ($\mathcal{O}(\log_2 N)$)

To prove that a specific telemetry frame $\mathcal{T}_m$ ($1 \le m \le N$) is an untampered member of the committed root $R_N$, the audit server provides an authentication path $\pi(m)$ consisting of the sibling hashes along the direct path from leaf $m$ to root $R_N$:

$$\pi(m) = \left\{ \text{sibling}(h_{d, \lfloor(m-1)/2^d\rfloor + 1}) \;\middle|\; d = 0, 1, \dots, K-1 \right\}$$

The verifier reconstructs the candidate root $\hat{R}$ by evaluating exactly $K = \lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ consecutive SHA-256 hashes:

$$\text{Time Complexity} = \mathcal{O}(\log_2 N), \qquad \text{Proof Payload Size} = 32 \cdot \lceil \log_2 N \rceil \text{ Bytes}$$

For an industrial flight recorder storing $N = 10^6$ telemetry frames ($\approx 16.7\text{ minutes}$ at $1000\text{ Hz}$), the audit path requires only $\lceil \log_2 10^6 \rceil = 20$ hashes ($640\text{ Bytes}$), verifying frame integrity in $< 15\,\mu\text{s}$.

#### Append-Only Consistency Invariant

To prove that an updated root $R_{N_2}$ strictly contains the historical log committed under $R_{N_1}$ ($N_1 < N_2$) without retroactive modification, the flight recorder emits a Merkle consistency proof of size $\le 2 \lceil \log_2 N_2 \rceil$. Under the standard assumption of SHA-256 collision resistance, the probability of an undetected ledger forgery is bounded by:

$$\mathbb{P}(\text{Undetected Tampering}) \le 2^{-256}$$

## 13. System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) Hazard Networks and Extreme Value Reliability Proofs

In whole-system verification and safety assurance, formal safety cases require connecting top-level system claims to rigorous control-theoretic hazard analyses and statistical extreme-value reliability proofs. This section establishes the mathematical foundations of STPA hazard networks and derives tail probability bounds using the Generalized Pareto Distribution.

### Formal Mathematical Formulation of STPA Hierarchical Control Structures

System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) models safety as a hierarchical dynamic control problem [@leveson2011engineering]. 

Let $\mathcal{L} = \{L_1, L_2, \dots, L_p\}$ denote the set of unacceptable **System Losses** (such as human injury, structural equipment destruction, or environmental damage).

A **System Hazard** $H_k \in \mathcal{H}$ is defined as a system state or set of conditions that, together with a worst-case set of environmental conditions, leads to a system loss:

$$H_k = \langle \mathcal{S}_k, \mathcal{C}_k \rangle \implies \bigcup_{i} L_i$$

where $\mathcal{S}_k \subset \mathcal{X}$ is the unsafe physical state space and $\mathcal{C}_k$ is the active environmental context.

The multi-rate, heterogeneous Physical AI architecture is modeled as a directed hierarchical control graph $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$:
* Vertices $\mathcal{V} = \{\text{Cloud}, \text{Host MPU}, \text{Edge NPU}, \text{Bare-Metal MCU}, \text{Actuators}, \text{Physical Plant}\}$ represent control entities and physical substrates.
* Directed edges $\mathcal{E} = \mathcal{U}_{\text{ctrl}} \cup \mathcal{Y}_{\text{fb}}$ represent control actions $\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{U}_{\text{ctrl}}$ descending the hierarchy and feedback measurements $\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{Y}_{\text{fb}}$ ascending the hierarchy.

Every control action $\mathbf{u}_j$ issued by controller $V_i$ is evaluated across the four canonical classes of **Unsafe Control Actions (UCAs)**:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{UCA}_{j,1}(\mathbf{x}, t) &= (\mathbf{u}_j(t) = \emptyset) \land \mathcal{P}_{\text{req}}(\mathbf{x}(t)) \quad &&(\text{Control Action Not Provided}) \\
\text{UCA}_{j,2}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, t) &= (\mathbf{u}_j(t) = \mathbf{u}_{\text{unsafe}}) \land \mathcal{P}_{\text{hazard}}(\mathbf{x}(t), \mathbf{u}_j) \quad &&(\text{Unsafe Action Provided}) \\
\text{UCA}_{j,3}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, t) &= (\mathbf{u}_j(t) \neq \emptyset) \land (t < t_{\text{early}} \lor t > t_{\text{late}}) \quad &&(\text{Action Too Early or Too Late}) \\
\text{UCA}_{j,4}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, \Delta t) &= (\Delta t < \Delta t_{\text{min}} \lor \Delta t > \Delta t_{\text{max}}) \quad &&(\text{Action Stopped Too Soon or Too Long})
\end{aligned}$$

where $\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x})$ denotes a Boolean predicate over continuous physical state space $\mathcal{X}$.

The STPA safety verification contract dictates that for every identified $\text{UCA}_{j,k}$, the system must incorporate a deterministic, hardware-isolated invariant enforcer:

$$\forall \text{UCA}_{j,k}, \quad \exists \mathcal{C}_{\text{barrier}}: \quad \text{Condition}(\text{UCA}_{j,k}) \implies \text{Trigger}(\text{Fallback Safety Interlock})$$

### Extreme Value Theory (EVT) and Peak-Over-Threshold Reliability Proofs

In safety-critical physical systems, nominal statistical distributions (such as Gaussian or Student-$t$ models) systematically underestimate tail risk. Catastrophic collisions occur at the extreme tail of the latency and tracking error distributions ($P_{99.999}$).

To rigorously prove that the probability of catastrophic hazard occurrence satisfies the top-level safety claim:

$$P(\text{Hazard}) < 10^{-6} \text{ per operating hour}$$

Physical AI applies **Extreme Value Theory (EVT)** using the **Peak-Over-Threshold (POT)** methodology [@coles2001introduction].

Let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_N$ be a sequence of independent and identically distributed physical error measurements (such as sense-to-actuation latency $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ or spatial clearance violation $\Delta d$) with underlying continuous distribution function $F(x)$.

Given a high threshold $u \in \mathbb{R}$, define the threshold exceedance variable $Y = X - u$ for $X > u$. The conditional excess distribution function $F_u(y)$ is:

$$F_u(y) = P(X - u \le y \mid X > u) = \frac{F(u + y) - F(u)}{1 - F(u)}$$

#### The Pickands-Balkema-de Haan Theorem and Asymptotic Proof

The fundamental theorem of Extreme Value Theory states that for a broad class of underlying distributions $F(x)$, as threshold $u$ approaches the upper endpoint $x_F = \sup\{x \mid F(x) < 1\}$, the conditional excess distribution $F_u(y)$ converges uniformly to the **Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD)**:

$$\lim_{u \to x_F} \sup_{0 \le y < x_F - u} \left| F_u(y) - G(y; \sigma(u), \xi) \right| = 0$$

where the Generalized Pareto cumulative distribution function $G(y; \sigma, \xi)$ is defined by:

$$G(y; \sigma, \xi) = \begin{cases}
1 - \left( 1 + \frac{\xi y}{\sigma} \right)^{-1/\xi} & \text{for } \xi \neq 0 \\
1 - \exp\left( -\frac{y}{\sigma} \right) & \text{for } \xi = 0
\end{cases}$$

parameterized by scale parameter $\sigma > 0$ and shape parameter (tail index) $\xi \in \mathbb{R}$, defined on support $y \ge 0$ for $\xi \ge 0$, and $0 \le y \le -\sigma/\xi$ for $\xi < 0$.

##### Formal Step-by-Step Mathematical Proof

1. **Maximum Domain of Attraction (MDA):** By the Fisher-Tippett-Gnedenko theorem, if the normalized maxima $M_n = \max(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ converge in distribution to a non-degenerate Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution $H_\xi(z) = \exp\left(-(1+\xi z)^{-1/\xi}\right)$, then there exist sequence normalizers $a_n > 0$ and $b_n \in \mathbb{R}$ such that:
   $$\lim_{n \to \infty} F^n(a_n z + b_n) = H_\xi(z)$$

2. **Logarithmic Expansion of the Tail:** Taking the natural logarithm of both sides:
   $$\lim_{n \to \infty} n \ln F(a_n z + b_n) = -(1 + \xi z)^{-1/\xi}$$
   Applying the first-order Taylor expansion $\ln F = \ln(1 - (1 - F)) \approx -(1 - F)$ for $F \to 1$:
   $$\lim_{n \to \infty} n \left( 1 - F(a_n z + b_n) \right) = (1 + \xi z)^{-1/\xi}$$

3. **Threshold Substitution:** Let threshold $u_n = b_n$ and excess $y = a_n z$ (so $z = y / a_n$). When $z = 0$, $n(1 - F(b_n)) \to 1$.
   The conditional excess tail probability is:
   $$1 - F_{u_n}(y) = P(X - u_n > y \mid X > u_n) = \frac{1 - F(u_n + y)}{1 - F(u_n)} = \frac{1 - F(b_n + a_n z)}{1 - F(b_n)}$$

4. **Asymptotic Convergence to GPD:** Taking the limit as $n \to \infty$ ($u \to x_F$):
   $$\lim_{n \to \infty} \left( 1 - F_{u_n}(y) \right) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n(1 - F(b_n + a_n z))}{n(1 - F(b_n))} = \frac{(1 + \xi z)^{-1/\xi}}{1} = \left( 1 + \frac{\xi y}{a_n} \right)^{-1/\xi}$$
   Setting the positive scaling function $\sigma(u) = a_n = \sigma_0 + \xi u$ yields the exact Generalized Pareto survival function:
   $$F_u(y) \longrightarrow 1 - \left( 1 + \frac{\xi y}{\sigma(u)} \right)^{-1/\xi} = G(y; \sigma(u), \xi) \quad \text{as } u \to x_F$$
   This completes the proof of uniform tail convergence. $\blacksquare$

* **$\xi > 0$ (Fréchet / Heavy-Tailed):** Models non-deterministic systems with operating system scheduling stalls and memory bus contention where tail latencies decay polynomially.
* **$\xi = 0$ (Gumbel / Exponential):** Models memoryless random processes.
* **$\xi < 0$ (Weibull / Bounded):** Models hard real-time systems with deterministic physical upper limits.

#### Derivation of the Tail Return Level for Safety Assurance

Let $N_u = \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{I}(X_i > u)$ denote the number of recorded exceedances above threshold $u$ in a sample of size $N$. The empirical probability of exceeding the threshold is $\hat{\zeta}_u = N_u / N$.

Combining the empirical threshold probability with the Generalized Pareto model yields the cumulative tail distribution for $x > u$:

$$P(X > x) = P(X > u) \cdot P(X - u > x - u \mid X > u) = \frac{N_u}{N} \left( 1 + \frac{\xi (x - u)}{\sigma} \right)^{-1/\xi}$$

Inverting this equation yields the **High-Quantile Safety Return Level** $x_p$ corresponding to extreme target failure probability $p$:

$$x_p = u + \frac{\sigma}{\xi} \left[ \left( \frac{N}{N_u} p \right)^{-\xi} - 1 \right]$$

For an embodied robot operating at control cadence $f_s = 1000\text{ Hz}$, one operating hour contains $N_{\text{hour}} = 3.6 \times 10^6$ execution cycles. A target hazard rate of $10^{-6}\text{ / hour}$ corresponds to a per-cycle failure probability of:

$$p_{\text{cycle}} = \frac{10^{-6}}{3.6 \times 10^6} = 2.78 \times 10^{-13}$$

Evaluating $x_{p_{\text{cycle}}}$ on empirical Hardware-in-the-Loop fault injection datasets provides the exact mathematical upper bound on worst-case latency or stopping distance required to substantiate the Claims-Arguments-Evidence safety case.

### Embedded C Implementation: STPA Runtime Monitor and POT Tail Estimator (`malloc = 0`)

The following C implementation evaluates runtime STPA hazard invariants and maintains online Peak-Over-Threshold extreme value statistics entirely in static SRAM without dynamic memory allocation:

```c
#include <math.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <string.h>

#define MAX_EXCEEDANCES 256

typedef struct {
    float clearance_m;          // Measured physical obstacle clearance
    float velocity_mps;         // Current operational velocity
    float latency_ms;           // Measured end-to-end transport latency
    float mu_friction_est;      // Real-time traction estimate
    bool  heartbeat_valid;      // Host MPU heartbeat status
    uint64_t timestamp_us;      // 64-bit PTP hardware timestamp
} stpa_plant_telemetry_t;

typedef struct {
    float u_threshold;          // POT analysis threshold (e.g. 35.0 ms)
    float exceedances[MAX_EXCEEDANCES]; // Ring buffer of tail values
    uint32_t exceedance_count;  // Total exceedances observed (N_u)
    uint32_t total_samples;     // Total execution cycles monitored (N)
    float sigma_est;            // Estimated GPD scale parameter
    float xi_est;               // Estimated GPD shape parameter (tail index)
} pot_estimator_t;

// Static workspace for zero heap allocation
static pot_estimator_t s_pot_latency;

// Initialize online Peak-Over-Threshold estimator
void pot_estimator_init(pot_estimator_t* pot, float threshold) {
    pot->u_threshold = threshold;
    pot->exceedance_count = 0;
    pot->total_samples = 0;
    pot->sigma_est = 5.0f; // Initial prior
    pot->xi_est = 0.15f;   // Heavy-tailed prior
    memset(pot->exceedances, 0, sizeof(pot->exceedances));
}

// Ingest sample and update tail statistics (WCET <= 1.5 us)
void pot_ingest_sample(pot_estimator_t* pot, float sample_val) {
    pot->total_samples++;
    if (sample_val > pot->u_threshold) {
        uint32_t idx = pot->exceedance_count % MAX_EXCEEDANCES;
        pot->exceedances[idx] = sample_val - pot->u_threshold;
        pot->exceedance_count++;
        
        // Online Probability-Weighted Moments (PWM) parameter update
        if (pot->exceedance_count >= 16) {
            uint32_t n = (pot->exceedance_count < MAX_EXCEEDANCES) ? pot->exceedance_count : MAX_EXCEEDANCES;
            float m0 = 0.0f;
            float m1 = 0.0f;
            for (uint32_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                m0 += pot->exceedances[i];
                m1 += pot->exceedances[i] * ((float)i / (float)n);
            }
            m0 /= (float)n;
            m1 /= (float)n;
            
            // GPD parameter estimators from moments
            if (m0 > 1e-4f && fabsf(m0 - 2.0f * m1) > 1e-4f) {
                pot->xi_est = (m0 - 4.0f * m1) / (m0 - 2.0f * m1);
                pot->sigma_est = (2.0f * m0 * m1) / (m0 - 2.0f * m1);
                if (pot->sigma_est < 0.1f) pot->sigma_est = 0.1f;
            }
        }
    }
}

// Compute high-quantile return level for target probability p (e.g., 1e-6)
float pot_compute_return_level(const pot_estimator_t* pot, float target_p) {
    if (pot->exceedance_count < 8 || pot->total_samples == 0) {
        return pot->u_threshold * 2.0f; // Conservative default before convergence
    }
    float zeta_u = (float)pot->exceedance_count / (float)pot->total_samples;
    if (target_p >= zeta_u) return pot->u_threshold;
    
    float ratio = (zeta_u / target_p);
    if (fabsf(pot->xi_est) < 1e-4f) {
        // Gumbel exponential limit
        return pot->u_threshold + pot->sigma_est * logf(ratio);
    } else {
        // Generalized Pareto general quantile
        return pot->u_threshold + (pot->sigma_est / pot->xi_est) * (powf(ratio, pot->xi_est) - 1.0f);
    }
}

// STPA Invariant Checker running in 1 kHz bare-metal ISR
bool evaluate_stpa_safety_invariants(
    const stpa_plant_telemetry_t* telem,
    uint8_t* trip_code_out
) {
    // Ingest latency sample into extreme value tracker
    pot_ingest_sample(&s_pot_latency, telem->latency_ms);
    
    // 1. Check UCA 1: Heartbeat missing or watchdog lease expired
    if (!telem->heartbeat_valid) {
        *trip_code_out = 0x01; // UCA_HEARTBEAT_EXPIRED
        return false;
    }
    
    // 2. Check UCA 2: Dynamic stopping clearance violation under active friction
    float effective_a_max = telem->mu_friction_est * 9.81f;
    if (effective_a_max < 0.5f) effective_a_max = 0.5f; // Physical minimum bound
    
    float d_react = telem->velocity_mps * (telem->latency_ms * 0.001f);
    float d_brake = (telem->velocity_mps * telem->velocity_mps) / (2.0f * effective_a_max);
    float d_stop_required = d_react + d_brake + 0.15f; // 15 cm safety buffer
    
    if (d_stop_required > telem->clearance_m) {
        *trip_code_out = 0x02; // UCA_CLEARANCE_BREACH
        return false;
    }
    
    // 3. Check UCA 3: Predicted extreme tail latency exceeds hard real-time budget
    float predicted_p9999_latency = pot_compute_return_level(&s_pot_latency, 1e-4f);
    if (predicted_p9999_latency > 65.0f) {
        *trip_code_out = 0x03; // UCA_TAIL_LATENCY_DERATE_REQUIRED
        // Flag warning to derate speed; does not trip hard stop immediately
    }
    
    *trip_code_out = 0x00; // All invariants satisfied
    return true;
}
```

## 14. Multi-Agent Decentralized Barrier Certificates and $SE(3)$ Lie Group Equivariance

This section provides formal proofs and embedded implementations for distributed multi-agent safety certificates and geometric symmetry constraints in physical foundation models.

### Multi-Agent Decentralized Control Barrier Functions (D-CBFs)

Consider a fleet of $N$ autonomous physical agents operating in a shared physical workspace. Each agent $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ possesses continuous control-affine dynamics:

$$\dot{\mathbf{x}}_i = f_i(\mathbf{x}_i) + g_i(\mathbf{x}_i)\mathbf{u}_i$$

where $\mathbf{x}_i = [\mathbf{p}_i^T, \mathbf{v}_i^T]^T \in \mathbb{R}^{n_i}$ is the agent state (position $\mathbf{p}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and velocity $\mathbf{v}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$) and $\mathbf{u}_i \in \mathcal{U}_i \subset \mathbb{R}^{m_i}$ is the control input (acceleration or motor force).

For any pair of agents $(i, j)$ with $i \ne j$, let $r_i$ and $r_j$ denote their respective physical bounding radii, and let $d_{\text{margin}}$ be a safety buffer. The minimum required physical separation is $R_{ij} = r_i + r_j + d_{\text{margin}}$. The pairwise spatial barrier certificate function $h_{ij}(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j): \mathbb{R}^{n_i} \times \mathbb{R}^{n_j} \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined as:

$$h_{ij}(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) = \|\mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{p}_j\|_2^2 - R_{ij}^2$$

The pairwise collision-free safe set is $\mathcal{C}_{ij} = \{ (\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) \mid h_{ij}(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) \ge 0 \}$. The collective fleet safe operating set $\mathcal{C}_{\text{fleet}}$ is the intersection across all pairs:

$$\mathcal{C}_{\text{fleet}} = \bigcap_{i=1}^N \bigcap_{j > i}^N \mathcal{C}_{ij}$$

### Reciprocating Collision Avoidance and Decentralized Safety Guarantees

Differentiating $h_{ij}(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)$ along the joint trajectories yields:

$$\dot{h}_{ij}(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j, \mathbf{u}_i, \mathbf{u}_j) = 2(\mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{p}_j)^T (\mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{v}_j) = \nabla_{\mathbf{x}_i} h_{ij} \left( f_i(\mathbf{x}_i) + g_i(\mathbf{x}_i)\mathbf{u}_i \right) + \nabla_{\mathbf{x}_j} h_{ij} \left( f_j(\mathbf{x}_j) + g_j(\mathbf{x}_j)\mathbf{u}_j \right)$$

Using Lie derivative notation:

$$\dot{h}_{ij} = L_{f_i} h_{ij} + L_{g_i} h_{ij} \mathbf{u}_i + L_{f_j} h_{ij} + L_{g_j} h_{ij} \mathbf{u}_j$$

To maintain forward invariance of $\mathcal{C}_{ij}$, the joint control input $(\mathbf{u}_i, \mathbf{u}_j)$ must satisfy:

$$L_{f_i} h_{ij} + L_{g_i} h_{ij} \mathbf{u}_i + L_{f_j} h_{ij} + L_{g_j} h_{ij} \mathbf{u}_j + \alpha(h_{ij}) \ge 0$$

where $\alpha(\cdot)$ is an extended class-$\mathcal{K}$ function (chosen as linear $\alpha(h) = \gamma h$ with $\gamma > 0$).

#### Reciprocating Responsibility Decomposition

In a decentralized fleet lacking a central coordinator, agent $i$ cannot command agent $j$'s control input $\mathbf{u}_j$. Under the **Reciprocating Collision Avoidance Principle**, each agent assumes equal responsibility for preserving the pairwise safety barrier:

$$\alpha_{ij}(h_{ij}) = \frac{1}{2} \alpha(h_{ij})$$

Agent $i$ enforces its local decentralized barrier constraint:

$$L_{f_i} h_{ij}(\mathbf{x}_i, \hat{\mathbf{x}}_j) + L_{g_i} h_{ij}(\mathbf{x}_i, \hat{\mathbf{x}}_j) \mathbf{u}_i + \frac{1}{2} \gamma h_{ij}(\mathbf{x}_i, \hat{\mathbf{x}}_j) \ge 0$$

Simultaneously, agent $j$ enforces its reciprocal constraint:

$$L_{f_j} h_{ij}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) + L_{g_j} h_{ij}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) \mathbf{u}_j + \frac{1}{2} \gamma h_{ij}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_i, \mathbf{x}_j) \ge 0$$

#### Theorem: Collective Forward Set Invariance under Reciprocating D-CBFs

If every agent $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ selects its local control action $\mathbf{u}_i$ from its admissible set:

$$\mathcal{U}_i(\mathbf{x}_i) = \left\{ \mathbf{u}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{m_i} \;\middle|\; L_{f_i} h_{ij} + L_{g_i} h_{ij} \mathbf{u}_i + \frac{1}{2}\gamma h_{ij} \ge 0, \quad \forall j \ne i \right\}$$

then the joint system trajectory satisfies:

$$\dot{h}_{ij} + \gamma h_{ij} = \left( L_{f_i} h_{ij} + L_{g_i} h_{ij} \mathbf{u}_i + \frac{1}{2}\gamma h_{ij} \right) + \left( L_{f_j} h_{ij} + L_{g_j} h_{ij} \mathbf{u}_j + \frac{1}{2}\gamma h_{ij} \right) \ge 0 + 0 = 0$$

Applying the Comparison Lemma, $h_{ij}(t) \ge h_{ij}(0) e^{-\gamma t} \ge 0$ for all $t \ge 0$. The collective safe operating set $\mathcal{C}_{\text{fleet}}$ is strictly forward invariant, guaranteeing zero inter-agent collisions across the entire fleet without centralized arbitration.

### Asynchronous State Estimation and Network Latency Margin Bounds

In realistic radio-frequency networks, agent $i$ receives position broadcasts from neighbor $j$ with transport delay $\tau_{ij} \in [0, \tau_{\text{max}}]$ and bounded packet drop probability.

Let $\hat{\mathbf{p}}_j(t) = \mathbf{p}_j(t - \tau_{ij}) + \mathbf{v}_j(t - \tau_{ij})\tau_{ij}$ be the dead-reckoned position estimate. Given a known maximum physical acceleration $a_{\text{max}}$, the state estimation error is bounded:

$$\|\mathbf{p}_j(t) - \hat{\mathbf{p}}_j(t)\|_2 \le \frac{1}{2} a_{\text{max}} \tau_{ij}^2 \le \frac{1}{2} a_{\text{max}} \tau_{\text{max}}^2 = \epsilon_{\text{pos}}(\tau_{\text{max}})$$

To guarantee forward invariance under network latency, agent $i$ inflates the effective pairwise collision radius:

$$R_{ij}^{\text{net}}(\tau_{\text{max}}) = r_i + r_j + d_{\text{margin}} + 2 \epsilon_{\text{pos}}(\tau_{\text{max}}) = r_i + r_j + d_{\text{margin}} + a_{\text{max}} \tau_{\text{max}}^2$$

Evaluating the D-CBF against the inflated radius $R_{ij}^{\text{net}}$ mathematically guarantees collision avoidance despite asynchronous communications.

### $SE(3)$ Lie Group Equivariance in Neural Physical Policies

In 3D physical manipulation and locomotion, the underlying laws of Newtonian mechanics are invariant under rigid coordinate transformations. A policy that learns to grasp an object at pose $\mathbf{T}_1 \in SE(3)$ should generalize directly when that same object is rotated and translated to pose $\mathbf{T}_2 = g \cdot \mathbf{T}_1$, where $g \in SE(3)$.

#### Mathematical Group Action on State and Action Spaces

Let $G = SE(3) = SO(3) \ltimes \mathbb{R}^3$ denote the Special Euclidean group. An element $g = (\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}) \in G$ consists of a 3D rotation matrix $\mathbf{R} \in SO(3)$ and a translation vector $\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^3$.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ denote the sensory observation space (point clouds, 3D feature embeddings, or depth tokens) and let $\mathcal{A}$ denote the physical action space (Cartesian end-effector waypoints or spatial wrench vectors). We define the group representations $\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(g): \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{X}$ and $\rho_{\mathcal{A}}(g): \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{A}$:

1. **On Observation Points $\mathbf{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}$:** $\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(g) \mathbf{P} = \mathbf{P} \mathbf{R}^T + \mathbf{1}_{N \times 1} \mathbf{t}^T$.
2. **On Commanded Trajectory Waypoints $\mathbf{p}_k \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and Orientations $\mathbf{R}_k \in SO(3)$:**
   $$\rho_{\mathcal{A}}(g)(\mathbf{p}_k, \mathbf{R}_k) = (\mathbf{R}\mathbf{p}_k + \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{R}\mathbf{R}_k)$$

#### Formal Definition of $SE(3)$-Equivariance

A neural policy $\pi_\theta: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{A}$ is strictly **$SE(3)$-equivariant** if the mapping commutes with the group action:

$$\pi_\theta(\rho_{\mathcal{X}}(g) \cdot \mathbf{O}) = \rho_{\mathcal{A}}(g) \cdot \pi_\theta(\mathbf{O}), \quad \forall g \in SE(3), \quad \forall \mathbf{O} \in \mathcal{X}$$

```
                rho_X(g)
       O ──────────────────────> g · O
       │                           │
       │                           │
pi_theta(O)                    pi_theta(g · O)
       │                           │
       v                           v
       A ──────────────────────> g · A
                rho_A(g)
```

When an unconstrained transformer or MLP processes physical observations, it must learn the effect of rotations empirically by consuming thousands of data augmentations. An $SE(3)$-equivariant architecture enforces this commutation structurally in its layer weights, guaranteeing that rotating the input scene rotates the predicted action trajectory identically by construction.

### Steerable Tensor Representations and Clebsch-Gordan Decompositions

To build neural layers that respect $SO(3)$ rotational symmetries, feature vectors at each 3D point are decomposed into direct sums of irreducible representations (irreps) of $SO(3)$:

$$V = \bigoplus_{l=0}^{l_{\text{max}}} \mathbb{R}^{2l + 1}$$

where $l$ is the rotation order:
* **$l = 0$ (Scalars, dimension 1):** Invariant under rotation (temperatures, masses, distances, grasp probabilities). $\rho_0(\mathbf{R}) = 1$.
* **$l = 1$ (Vectors, dimension 3):** Standard 3D vectors (positions, velocities, forces). $\rho_1(\mathbf{R}) = \mathbf{R}$.
* **$l = 2$ (Tensors, dimension 5):** Symmetric traceless $3 \times 3$ matrices (stress tensors, quadric surfaces, inertia moments). $\rho_2(\mathbf{R}) = \mathbf{D}^2(\mathbf{R})$, where $\mathbf{D}^l(\mathbf{R})$ is the $(2l+1) \times (2l+1)$ Wigner D-matrix.

#### Formal Group-Theoretic Tensor Product Reduction Proof

Let $V_{l_1}$ and $V_{l_2}$ denote vector spaces transforming under irreducible representations $\mathbf{D}^{l_1}(\mathbf{R})$ and $\mathbf{D}^{l_2}(\mathbf{R})$ of dimensions $2l_1 + 1$ and $2l_2 + 1$, respectively.

1. **Product Representation Structure:** The tensor product representation space $V_{l_1} \otimes V_{l_2}$ has dimension $(2l_1 + 1)(2l_2 + 1)$ and transforms under rotation $\mathbf{R} \in SO(3)$ according to the Kronecker product matrix:
   $$\rho_{l_1 \otimes l_2}(\mathbf{R}) = \mathbf{D}^{l_1}(\mathbf{R}) \otimes \mathbf{D}^{l_2}(\mathbf{R})$$

2. **Complete Reducibility via Lie Algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$:** The Lie algebra commutation relations $[J_i, J_j] = i \epsilon_{ijk} J_k$ and the total angular momentum Casimir invariant $J^2 = J_x^2 + J_y^2 + J_z^2$ dictate that the product space decomposes into a direct sum of distinct irreducible representations:
   $$V_{l_1} \otimes V_{l_2} \cong \bigoplus_{l = |l_1 - l_2|}^{l_1 + l_2} V_l$$

3. **Clebsch-Gordan Change-of-Basis Matrix:** The unitary transformation matrix $\mathbf{C}$ mapping the uncoupled tensor product basis $\{|l_1 m_1\rangle \otimes |l_2 m_2\rangle\}$ to the coupled irreducible basis $\{|l m\rangle\}$ consists of the **Clebsch-Gordan coefficients** $C_{(l_1, m_1)(l_2, m_2)}^{(l, m)} = \langle l_1 m_1; l_2 m_2 \mid l m \rangle$:
   $$|l, m\rangle = \sum_{m_1=-l_1}^{l_1} \sum_{m_2=-l_2}^{l_2} C_{(l_1, m_1)(l_2, m_2)}^{(l, m)} \left( |l_1, m_1\rangle \otimes |l_2, m_2\rangle \right)$$

4. **Equivariance Commutation Identity:** Applying the unitary matrix $\mathbf{C}$ block-diagonalizes the Kronecker product:
   $$\mathbf{C} \left( \mathbf{D}^{l_1}(\mathbf{R}) \otimes \mathbf{D}^{l_2}(\mathbf{R}) \right) \mathbf{C}^\dagger = \bigoplus_{l = |l_1 - l_2|}^{l_1 + l_2} \mathbf{D}^l(\mathbf{R})$$
   Therefore, combining geometric features $\mathbf{v}_1 \in V_{l_1}$ and $\mathbf{v}_2 \in V_{l_2}$ via the Clebsch-Gordan tensor product:
   $$(\mathbf{v}_1 \otimes_{\text{CG}} \mathbf{v}_2)_m^l = \sum_{m_1=-l_1}^{l_1} \sum_{m_2=-l_2}^{l_2} C_{(l_1, m_1)(l_2, m_2)}^{(l, m)} v_{1, m_1}^{l_1} v_{2, m_2}^{l_2}$$
   guarantees that every hidden layer in the neural policy commutes exactly with the $SO(3)$ rotation group:
   $$\mathbf{W} \left( \mathbf{D}^{l_1}(\mathbf{R})\mathbf{v}_1 \otimes_{\text{CG}} \mathbf{D}^{l_2}(\mathbf{R})\mathbf{v}_2 \right) = \mathbf{D}^l(\mathbf{R}) \mathbf{W} \left( \mathbf{v}_1 \otimes_{\text{CG}} \mathbf{v}_2 \right), \quad \forall \mathbf{R} \in SO(3)$$
   This proves structural equivariance by construction. $\blacksquare$

### Sample Complexity Scaling Proof in Physical Space

Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the class of $L$-Lipschitz continuous robotic manipulation policies mapping a bounded workspace $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ to bounded action trajectories in $[-1, 1]^d$.

#### Non-Equivariant Hypothesis Space Complexity

For a standard unconstrained neural network (such as a Vision Transformer or MLP), the $\epsilon$-covering number of the policy hypothesis space $\mathcal{H}_{\text{standard}}$ under the infinity norm satisfies:

$$\log \mathcal{N}\left(\epsilon, \mathcal{H}_{\text{standard}}, \|\cdot\|_\infty\right) = \mathcal{O}\left( \left(\frac{L}{\epsilon}\right)^{d_{\text{in}}} \right)$$

where $d_{\text{in}} = 3K$ represents the dimensionality of $K$ spatial input points. The number of physical demonstrations $M_{\text{standard}}$ required to achieve generalization error $\le \epsilon$ scales as:

$$M_{\text{standard}} = \Omega\left( \frac{1}{\epsilon^2} \left(\frac{L}{\epsilon}\right)^{3K} \right)$$

#### Equivariant Hypothesis Space Complexity

When the policy space is constrained to the $SE(3)$-equivariant subspace $\mathcal{H}_{\text{equiv}} \subset \mathcal{H}_{\text{standard}}$, any function $f \in \mathcal{H}_{\text{equiv}}$ is uniquely determined by its values on the orbit quotient space $\Omega / SE(3)$.

Because the group $SE(3)$ has dimension $\dim(SE(3)) = 6$ (3 translational and 3 rotational degrees of freedom), the effective input manifold dimensionality is reduced from $3K$ to $3K - 6$ for $K \ge 3$. Furthermore, the volume of the search space is divided by the Haar volume of the compact rotation group $|SO(3)| = 8\pi^2$:

$$\log \mathcal{N}\left(\epsilon, \mathcal{H}_{\text{equiv}}, \|\cdot\|_\infty\right) = \mathcal{O}\left( \frac{1}{|SO(3)|} \left(\frac{L}{\epsilon}\right)^{3K - 6} \right)$$

For 3D robotic grasping where the target object can appear in arbitrary $SE(3)$ poses, the sample complexity ratio evaluates to:

$$\frac{M_{\text{equiv}}}{M_{\text{standard}}} \approx \frac{1}{|SO(3)| \cdot (\text{discretization steps})^{3}} \approx \frac{1}{100} \text{ to } \frac{1}{1000}$$

This mathematical bound explains why $SE(3)$-equivariant foundation policies (such as Equivariant Diffusion Policy and Perceiver-Actor) achieve $95\%$ pick-and-place success rates with only $20\text{--}50$ physical demonstrations, whereas non-equivariant models require $2{,}000\text{--}5{,}000$ trials to learn spatial rotational invariance.

### Embedded C Implementation of Decentralized CBF Filter (`malloc = 0`)

The following C implementation runs at $1000\text{ Hz}$ on an ARM Cortex-M7 microcontroller. It filters an agent's candidate acceleration command against up to 8 neighboring agents using reciprocating D-CBFs in static DTCM SRAM:

```c
#include <math.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <string.h>

#define MAX_NEIGHBORS 8
#define STATE_DIM     3  // 3D Cartesian coordinates

typedef struct {
    float pos[STATE_DIM];     // Agent current position (meters)
    float vel[STATE_DIM];     // Agent current velocity (m/s)
    float radius;             // Physical bounding radius (meters)
    float a_max;              // Maximum acceleration limit (m/s^2)
    float gamma;              // CBF class-K linear parameter (e.g. 2.0 1/s)
    float d_margin;           // Static margin buffer (meters)
} agent_state_t;

typedef struct {
    float pos[STATE_DIM];     // Estimated neighbor position (meters)
    float vel[STATE_DIM];     // Estimated neighbor velocity (m/s)
    float radius;             // Neighbor bounding radius (meters)
    float latency_s;          // Age of neighbor packet (seconds)
    bool active;              // Neighbor presence flag
} neighbor_track_t;

typedef struct {
    float u_cand[STATE_DIM];  // Candidate acceleration proposal (m/s^2)
    float u_safe[STATE_DIM];  // Filtered safe acceleration output (m/s^2)
    int active_violations;    // Count of modified barrier constraints
} dcbf_result_t;

// Static zero-heap workspace for reciprocating D-CBF evaluation
static float s_A_cbf[MAX_NEIGHBORS][STATE_DIM];
static float s_b_cbf[MAX_NEIGHBORS];

// Evaluate reciprocating D-CBF filter (WCET <= 22 microseconds on Cortex-M7)
bool filter_multimodal_dcbf(
    const agent_state_t* self,
    const neighbor_track_t neighbors[MAX_NEIGHBORS],
    int num_neighbors,
    const float u_cand[STATE_DIM],
    dcbf_result_t* result
) {
    // 1. Initialize output with unconstrained candidate proposal
    for (int d = 0; d < STATE_DIM; d++) {
        result->u_safe[d] = u_cand[d];
    }
    result->active_violations = 0;

    int num_constraints = 0;

    // 2. Build pairwise reciprocating D-CBF linear constraints: A_cbf * u_self >= b_cbf
    for (int k = 0; k < num_neighbors && k < MAX_NEIGHBORS; k++) {
        if (!neighbors[k].active) continue;

        // Position difference vector: r_ij = p_self - p_neighbor
        float r_ij[STATE_DIM];
        float dist_sq = 0.0f;
        for (int d = 0; d < STATE_DIM; d++) {
            r_ij[d] = self->pos[d] - neighbors[k].pos[d];
            dist_sq += r_ij[d] * r_ij[d];
        }

        // Inflate safety radius for packet transport latency
        float eps_latency = 0.5f * self->a_max * (neighbors[k].latency_s * neighbors[k].latency_s);
        float R_min = self->radius + neighbors[k].radius + self->d_margin + (2.0f * eps_latency);
        float R_min_sq = R_min * R_min;

        // Barrier value: h_ij = ||r_ij||^2 - R_min^2
        float h_ij = dist_sq - R_min_sq;

        // Relative velocity: v_ij = v_self - v_neighbor
        float v_ij[STATE_DIM];
        float r_dot_v = 0.0f;
        for (int d = 0; d < STATE_DIM; d++) {
            v_ij[d] = self->vel[d] - neighbors[k].vel[d];
            r_dot_v += r_ij[d] * v_ij[d];
        }

        // Time derivative: h_dot = 2 * r_ij^T * v_ij
        // Control derivative: L_g h_ij = 2 * r_ij^T (since p_ddot_self = u_self)
        // Reciprocating split: L_g * u_self >= -2 * r_ij^T * v_ij - 0.5 * gamma * h_ij
        for (int d = 0; d < STATE_DIM; d++) {
            s_A_cbf[num_constraints][d] = 2.0f * r_ij[d];
        }
        s_b_cbf[num_constraints] = -2.0f * r_dot_v - 0.5f * self->gamma * h_ij;

        num_constraints++;
    }

    // 3. Project candidate control vector onto half-spaces via minimal perturbation
    for (int c = 0; c < num_constraints; c++) {
        float a_dot_u = 0.0f;
        float norm_a_sq = 0.0f;
        for (int d = 0; d < STATE_DIM; d++) {
            a_dot_u += s_A_cbf[c][d] * result->u_safe[d];
            norm_a_sq += s_A_cbf[c][d] * s_A_cbf[c][d];
        }

        float violation = s_b_cbf[c] - a_dot_u; // A * u >= b  --> violation = b - A*u
        if (violation > 1e-4f && norm_a_sq > 1e-8f) {
            // Apply single-constraint orthogonal projection: u = u + (violation / ||a||^2) * a
            float step = violation / norm_a_sq;
            for (int d = 0; d < STATE_DIM; d++) {
                result->u_safe[d] += step * s_A_cbf[c][d];
            }
            result->active_violations++;
        }
    }

    // 4. Enforce physical actuator acceleration limits
    float u_norm_sq = 0.0f;
    for (int d = 0; d < STATE_DIM; d++) {
        u_norm_sq += result->u_safe[d] * result->u_safe[d];
    }
    if (u_norm_sq > self->a_max * self->a_max) {
        float scale = self->a_max / sqrtf(u_norm_sq);
        for (int d = 0; d < STATE_DIM; d++) {
            result->u_safe[d] *= scale;
        }
    }

    return (result->active_violations == 0);
}
```
